newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Mandela urges Asia to invest in Southern Africa.
newsitem.headline: Mandela urges Asia to invest in Southern Africa.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela issued a passionate appeal to Asia on Thursday to see Southern Africa as a lucrative place in which to invest and a "geographical anchor" for trade with South America.

"Southern Africa today constitutes one of the most exciting regions of the world; a region endowed with abundant mineral resources, a market of over 100 million people, great tourist potential, democracy and peace," he said.
"This region has the potential to be the geographic anchor of new relations among Asia, Africa and Latin America," he said in a speech at the end of a two-day visit to Singapore.
Mandela next visits Malaysia, where he will wind up a four-nation tour of Southeast Asia aimed at promoting links between Africa and Asia.
Mandela said he wanted to rebuild cultural and trade ties between two regions he said had been destroyed by European colonisation of Africa.

"We are driven by a deep desire to rekindle old relationships. We yearn to rebuild what was destroyed. We seek to forge strong multilateral ties among our nations under the new and more favourable conditions of freedom, technological advance and peace."

Mandela urged Asian investors to hurry to South Africa, where economic reforms had opened up "massive mega-projects in mineral processing, petrochemical industries, telecommunications, car manufacturing, tourism, transportation and other infrastructure".
"In all these areas, the contribution of Singaporean and other investors will be critical," he said.

There were "opportunities for large profit margins, the advantage of a sophisticated banking system, the availability of a developed communications network, the freedom to repatriate profits and the advantage of tax holidays in certain designated areas," he said.
Mandela also called on 14 nations, including South Africa, meeting in Mauritius this week to speed up their bid to form an Indian Ocean Rim economic grouping.
"The idea of the Rim should be pursued with vigour," he said.

"In our interaction with states in Latin America, there is a conviction that the Indian Ocean Rim should be a precursor to similar relations between us and that part of the world," Mandela told an audience of officials, business leaders and scholars.

"There is a conviction too that such relations are important, not only in terms of the mutual benefits that they will bring our peoples, but also because they should help redefine the world balance as we know it," he said.
